tests.title: Tender values around the competitive-tender threshold
tests.question: Is there excess mass just below the threshold that triggers competitive tender?
tests.headline: No spike at the $250k line — just-below and just-above mass are balanced
tests.verdict: No Operation-Royston fingerprint: the amount distribution is a smooth small-jobs decay with no pile-up against the threshold.

tests.title: Repeat winners and big-dollar incumbents
tests.question: Is any supplier both a frequent repeat-winner and a big-dollar incumbent?
tests.headline: Most-recurring firm (Leoheaney) appears in 5 distinct years
tests.verdict: No entrenched big-dollar incumbent: the repeat-winners are mundane low-value equipment/cartage rebids, not the firms that capture the dollars.

tests.title: Single-source and direct-negotiation share
tests.question: What share of tenders had no competitive field?
tests.headline: Not computable on this corpus
tests.verdict: Tenders carry no competitive-field metadata (number of respondents) in this corpus, so single-source concentration can't be measured — flagged for re-extraction.

tests.title: Tender awards by contractor
tests.question: Is tendered spend concentrated, and how much is awarded confidentially?
tests.headline: $119.6M across 214 named firms; 23% of dollars redacted; top-10 take 47%
tests.verdict: Concentration is the nature of big civil contracts and the supplier base is broad; the watch-item is the redacted share (a transparency issue), not capture.

tests.title: Declared interests on tender awards
tests.question: When council awards a tender, is a conflict declared — and does the winner ever match a councillor's known connections?
tests.headline: Tender-award votes declare an interest just 1.74% of the time (below the 3.75% chamber base) — 2 raw decider↔winner surname collision(s) across 412 named awards, unconfirmed
tests.verdict: 2 raw surname collision(s) were found between a tender winner and a voting councillor — a name match against a councillor's surname, not a confirmed relationship; resolving one needs the underlying minute text (see the drill-down for names, firms, and provenance).
tests.base_rate: 3.75% chamber-wide declared-interest rate; 412 named awards vs 198 voting-councillor surnames

tests.title: Recusal following a declared interest
tests.question: When an interest is declared, is it *managed* — i.e. does the member recuse?
tests.headline: Declaring lifts recusal 83×, but members still stay and vote 75.0% of the time
tests.verdict: Disclosure works at the first step; the identify–disclose–manage chain breaks at the manage limb.

tests.title: Recusal rate before, during and after external scrutiny
tests.question: Did stepping out of serious conflicts change around external scrutiny?
tests.headline: Must-leave recusal fell from 87.1% before scrutiny to 66.7% after (peaked at 100.0% during it)
tests.verdict: Financial-only recusal (leaving is mandatory) moved 100.0%→100.0% (n=1) over the same window — too few post-scrutiny financial declarations to confirm or rule out a confound from a shift in which interest type gets declared.
tests.base_rate: leaving is legally mandatory for financial/proximity interests

tests.title: Declaration rate of council-appointed delegates
tests.question: When a councillor is Council's own appointed delegate/board member on an external body, do they declare an interest before voting on that body's business — the same disclosure regime a private supplier relationship gets?
tests.headline: Institutional delegates declare ~0% on their own body's business (public role, correctly) — the one body with genuine personal stakes, Ocean Gardens (Inc) Board of Management, declares 5/21 (23.8%), backed by 60 corpus-wide mentions — DIRECTIONAL, thin n
tests.verdict: The one channel where councillors could plausibly hold an undeclared personal stake in an external body's business — their own Council-appointed delegate role — comes back clean, and the split is explicable rather than a gap: institutional delegation (Mindarie Regional Council 0/15 (0.0%); Tamala Park Regional Council 0/2 (0.0%)) correctly attracts near-zero declarations, while Ocean Gardens (Inc) Board of Management, the one body some appointees hold a genuine private stake in, shows real declare-and-recuse behaviour at a materially higher rate, corroborated by 60 corpus-wide declaration mentions vs 1–3 for the institutional bodies. Every per-body n is thin (2–21 affiliated votes) — read this as a directional, explanatory pattern across three bodies, not a precise rate for any one of them.
tests.base_rate: other councillors' declared-interest rate on the SAME motions: Mindarie Regional Council 1.3%; Tamala Park Regional Council 11.1%; Ocean Gardens (Inc) Board of Management 3.7%

tests.title: Approval rate by development value
tests.question: Does approval rate vary with the estimated value of the development?
tests.headline: Approval by value quartile (low→high): 74/74/69/74%
tests.verdict: Flat across value quartiles — big developers get neither an easier ride nor extra scrutiny.

tests.title: Approval rate by applicant frequency
tests.question: Do repeat builders/agents get approved at a higher rate than one-shot applicants?
tests.headline: Approval by applicant frequency: 1×=82% · 2–3=72% · 4–6=84% · 7+=83%
tests.verdict: No repeat-player advantage — frequent applicants win no more than first-timers.

tests.title: Refusal rate by objection count
tests.question: Does refusal rise with the number of residents objecting to an application?
tests.headline: Refusal climbs 18.8% → 50.0% from no objectors to 5+
tests.verdict: A clean dose–response: a lone objection is noise, but coordinated numbers move outcomes — engagement works, even if a single letter does not.

tests.title: Departures from the officer recommendation
tests.principle: CIPFA-F · the 'visible contest is theatre' prior
tests.question: How often does council depart from the officer recommendation?
tests.headline: Council adopted the officer recommendation 97.0% of the time
tests.verdict: Near-total ratification means the substantive decision is upstream, in who writes the recommendation — the most important caveat on every voting finding.

tests.title: Outcomes on contested votes
tests.question: On contested votes, how unequal is who actually wins — and is it accountable?
tests.headline: Contested-vote win rates span 41–92% between councillors
tests.verdict: A real hidden hierarchy behind near-unanimous votes — but one that turns over at elections rather than ossifying, so it is electorally accountable.

tests.title: Oversight-committee membership against chamber win rates
tests.question: Does membership on the council's Audit Committee / CEO Performance Review Committee skew toward the chamber's habitual winners, or draw broadly — including from its habitual dissenters?
tests.headline: 31 distinct councillors have ever sat on an oversight body; appointee win rate 73.28% (n=7160) vs non-appointee 73.13% (n=3707) — a 0.2 pp gap, not meaningfully distinguishable
tests.verdict: No self-appointment of the powerful to watch themselves: the oversight-body appointee list's win-rate spread (31.0–92.5%) runs almost the full range of the chamber, from its most consistent winners among appointees down to some of the corpus's most frequent dissenters. CIPFA-A's internal audit/oversight-function principle is met on this reading; era-pooled, so a modern-era shift could still hide in the aggregate.

tests.title: Share of carried motions drawing dissent
tests.principle: CIPFA-B — how the chamber conducts business
tests.question: What share of carried motions drew at least one dissenting vote, over time?
tests.headline: 9.1% of carried motions drew a dissenting vote (chamber-wide)
tests.verdict: Mostly-unanimous on the surface; the contested share moves with the political era rather than holding constant.

tests.title: Dissent rate on the Mayor's motions against backbench motions
tests.question: Do the Mayor's own motions get an easier ride than backbench motions?
tests.headline: Mayoral motions drew dissent 21.8% of the time vs 8.3% for backbench motions
tests.verdict: The opposite of chair capture: the chamber votes against its own Mayor at least as often as backbench motions — the most powerful member earns no deference at the gavel.

tests.title: Sponsorship and voting blocs across electoral terms
tests.question: Do voting/sponsorship blocs persist across electoral terms (an entrenched bloc)?
tests.headline: A 2000s old-guard sponsorship clique existed and fragmented in 2008; no durable bloc in the modern council
tests.verdict: Working alliances are real and visible in who-seconds-whom, but the persistence test found no entrenched modern faction — the structure reshuffles each election.

tests.title: Tenure and turnover
tests.question: How entrenched is the chamber — long-server-heavy, or renewing?
tests.headline: Median service 9.5 years; 17 served 15+; longest 30.8y
tests.verdict: Stability with institutional memory, but a long-server-heavy tail that is an entrenchment risk worth watching.

tests.title: Dissent rate in a councillor's first year against later years
tests.question: Do councillors dissent at a different rate in their first year than later?
tests.headline: Dissent in first 12 months 22.5% vs 17.2% later
tests.verdict: No systematic freshman effect once cohort era is accounted for — new members behave much like veterans (the rigorous per-councillor test was a clean null).

tests.title: Dissent rate in the pre-election window
tests.question: Is dissent higher in the pre-election window than the rest of the cycle?
tests.headline: Pre-election dissent 19.4% vs 17.2% otherwise
tests.verdict: A small, confound-prone difference — no strong electoral-cycle positioning effect.

tests.title: Absence from votes, split by recusal and non-attendance
tests.question: What share of cast-vote opportunities are ABSENT, and is that recusal or disengagement?
tests.headline: 1.2% of vote rows are ABSENT — 76% of those are lawful recusal, only 24% genuine non-attendance (0.3% of all votes)
tests.verdict: The single ABSENT figure is dominated by councillors stepping out on declared conflicts, not disengagement: genuine non-attendance is a fraction of a percent of votes — an attendance strength once the recusal share is separated out.

tests.title: Share of decided items closed to the public
tests.question: What share of decided items is confidential, and is it rising?
tests.headline: 2.4% confidential at baseline, spiking to 17.2% in 2020
tests.verdict: A strong baseline openness rate with a spike that stands out from it; the concern is the scale and timing of that spike, not a habit of secrecy.

tests.title: Tender values, confidential against open
tests.question: Do confidential tenders carry higher dollar values than open ones?
tests.headline: Confidential tenders run a $313,495 median vs $108,861 open (~2.9×) — DIRECTIONAL, n=16
tests.verdict: The contracts residents can least scrutinise are systematically the largest — confidentiality is often lawful, so this is a visibility concern, not impropriety.

tests.title: Subject matter of confidential items
tests.question: Does confidentiality track lawful statutory grounds or politically contentious topics?
tests.headline: Confidentiality concentrates on lawful grounds (Commercial-in-conf 23%, lift 4.97×); contentious 'named development' is the LEAST closed (1.6%, lift 0.36×)
tests.verdict: Closure tracks the categories the law exists to protect (commercial-in-confidence, tenders, HR, legal, land contracts); the most politically sensitive category — named developments — is the most OPEN, not the most closed. Keyword themes are coarse, and any error biases toward the null (over-counting development closures).

tests.title: Tender spend by month of the budget year
tests.question: Do tender dollars cluster into the final months of the budget cycle?
tests.headline: December holds 13% of tender dollars (42 awards) vs ~8% expected
tests.verdict: A modest end-of-year bump consistent with normal capital timing, not a dramatic use-it-or-lose-it dump.

tests.title: Reserve balances over time
tests.question: Are reserves being depleted (the s.114 precursor)?
tests.headline: Not computable on this corpus
tests.verdict: An investment-portfolio series exists in the minutes (peaked ~$73M in 2018) but the ~24 irregular free-text snapshots can't be normalised to a defensible reserve trend yet — needs a finance-aware re-extraction.

tests.title: Public questions, deputations and petitions over time
tests.question: What is the volume and trend of public questions, deputations and petitions?
tests.headline: 4,993 recorded public engagements (questions, deputations, petitions) · ~190/yr recently
tests.verdict: Public participation is channelled through questions, deputations and petitions; the volume tracks the political temperature rather than a steady civic baseline.

tests.title: Contested-vote rate at meetings with a deputation
tests.question: Do meetings with a public deputation see more contested votes?
tests.headline: Contestation 9.5% with a deputation vs 7.4% without
tests.verdict: A small gap, confounded by busy meetings having both more deputations and more motions — no strong effect.

tests.title: Public questions taken on notice against answered in the meeting
tests.principle: CIPFA-B — openness & stakeholder engagement · Nolan Accountability
tests.question: What share of public questions are deferred rather than answered in the meeting, over time?
tests.headline: Deferral of public questions rose from 4.3% before scrutiny to 15.7% during it (peak 26.8% in 2020), still elevated at 11.2% after
tests.verdict: Most public questions are answered live, but during and after the scrutiny window they were increasingly deferred to 'on notice' — a measurable dip in in-room accountability. 'On notice' is lawful and often appropriate, so this is a responsiveness concern, not impropriety; the classifier is conservative, so the deferral share is a floor.
